How to price a job: markup vs margin for electrical, plumbing and HVAC business owners.
Want a 40% margin on $1,000 in cost? Divide by 0.6: $1,000 / 0.6 = $1,666.67.

Price = Cost / (1 - margin)

A 50% markup on $1,000 makes a $1,500 price, and the $500 is one third of it: a 33.3% margin, not 50% (Xero; Sal Alfano, JLC). Markup is on cost. Margin is on price. A real 50% margin takes a 100% markup ($1,000 cost, $2,000 quote).

youtube.title: How to Price a Job: Markup vs Margin for Electrical, Plumbing and HVAC Owners
youtube.description:
How to price a job: markup vs margin for electrical, plumbing and HVAC business owners.
Want a 40% margin on $1,000 in cost? Divide by 0.6: $1,000 / 0.6 = $1,666.67.
A 50% markup on $1,000 in cost makes a $1,500 price. The $500 is one third of the price, so the margin is 33.3%, not 50%. A real 50% margin takes a 100% markup: $1,000 in cost, $2,000 on the quote. Sources: Xero glossary, "Margin vs markup" (2026), https://www.xero.com/us/glossary/margin-vs-markup/ ; Sal Alfano, "Markup vs. Margin," JLC, https://www.jlconline.com/business/markup-vs-margin_o/

Price from the margin you want:
1. Pick the margin, say 40%.
2. Take 1 minus the margin: for 40%, that is 0.6.
3. Price = Cost / (1 - margin): $1,000 / 0.6 = $1,666.67.
4. Check it: $666.67 / $1,666.67 = 40%.

Markup is on cost. Margin is on price. Margin isn't take-home pay: it still has to cover your overhead and your pay. Send this to whoever sets your prices.
